precepts.text: The Most High divided the nations and separated the sons of Adam by the number of the children of Israel; Jacob is His portion.
precepts.point: After Babel the Most High sent every family back to where it was supposed to be: Ham to his place, Shem to his, Japheth to his.

note.label: Genesis 11: Babel and the Separation of the Nations

precepts.why:
The people being one at Babel was not going to produce righteousness. Nothing would be restrained from what they imagined to do, and it would be evil, so the Most High confounded their language and scattered them. There has never been a doctrine of all nations holding hands as one in the scriptures.

“Remember the days of old, consider the years of many generations: ask thy father, and he will shew thee; thy elders, and they will tell thee. When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel. For the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.”

The Most High divided the nations their inheritance and separated the sons of Adam, setting the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel; Jacob is his portion. After Babel he sent every family back to where it was supposed to be: Ham to his place, Shem to his, Japheth to his.

precepts.text: The man of sin exalts himself above all that is called God, sitting as God; the spirit of Nimrod all over again.
precepts.point: After Babel the Most High sent every family back to where it was supposed to be: Ham to his place, Shem to his, Japheth to his.

note.label: Genesis 11: Babel and the Separation of the Nations

precepts.why:
The man of sin opposes what the Most High did at Babel. “Let no man deceive you by any means: for that day shall not come, except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition; Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God.”

He exalts himself above all that is called God, gathers all nations to himself as one, and deifies himself, making God and the Messiah after his own image. That is the same thing Nimrod did in the land of Shinar, when the people were one and began to build the city and the tower. It is the spirit of Nimrod all over again, and the Most High scattered it the first time.

precepts.text: A just man is one that does that which is lawful and right.
precepts.point: Lot was a just man. To be just means to do that which is lawful and right, a commandment keeper; righteous Lot was vexed from day to day with the unlawful deeds of the wicked.

note.label: Genesis 11: Babel and the Separation of the Nations

precepts.why:
Haran begat Lot, and Lot was a just man. What just means: “But if a man be just, and do that which is lawful and right.”

To be just is to do that which is lawful and right, a commandment keeper. That is the Lot who went forth with Terah and Abram from Ur of the Chaldees, Ur meaning fire and the Chaldees being Babylon, the area Abram was born in and called out of.

precepts.text: Just Lot was a righteous man, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked.
precepts.point: Lot was a just man. To be just means to do that which is lawful and right, a commandment keeper; righteous Lot was vexed from day to day with the unlawful deeds of the wicked.

note.label: Genesis 11: Babel and the Separation of the Nations

precepts.why:
Peter calls him “just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked: (For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds;)”. Lot, the son of Haran who came out of Ur of the Chaldees with Abram, was a just man, one who did that which is lawful and right, and righteous Lot was vexed from day to day with the unlawful deeds of the wicked.

“The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished.” He delivered just Lot, and he reserves the unjust for judgment.

precepts.text: Haran begat Lot; Lot was Abram's nephew.
precepts.point: Their substance was so great they could not dwell together. That substance came from Egypt, where Pharaoh entreated Abram well for Sarai's sake and gave him sheep, oxen, servants, and camels; the maidservants from Egypt are where Hagar comes from.

note.label: Genesis 13: The Peacemaker and the Promise

precepts.why:
Lot was Abram’s nephew. “Terah begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran; and Haran begat Lot.” Haran was Abram’s brother, so Lot, the son of Haran, is the brother’s son who went with Abram.

That is who is in the strife of Genesis 13. Lot “also, which went with Abram, had flocks, and herds, and tents”, and the two households, uncle and nephew, had grown so great that “the land was not able to bear them, that they might dwell together.”

precepts.text: Sarai was barren from the beginning; she had no child.
precepts.point: Is any thing too hard for the Lord? The barren woman is made a joyful mother of children. Through faith Sarah received strength to conceive when she was past age, and Abraham, as good as dead at a hundred, staggered not at the promise but was strong in faith, fully persuaded that what He had promised He was able to perform.

note.label: Genesis 18: The Promise of Isaac and the Cry of Sodom

precepts.why:
Sarah did not become barren in old age; she was barren from the beginning. “But Sarai was barren; she had no child.” Now Abraham and Sarah were old and well stricken in age, and “it ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women.”

That is why she laughed within herself at the promise of a son. Barren from the start, and now past age. But is any thing too hard for the Lord?

precepts.text: Terah took Abram from Ur of the Chaldees to go into Canaan, and they came unto Haran and dwelt there; Jacob's road runs back to the family's old dwelling.
precepts.point: This is the same ground the family had already covered. Isaac charged Jacob to go to Padanaram to the house of Bethuel, and generations earlier Terah had brought Abram from Ur of the Chaldees up along the Euphrates, and they came unto Haran and dwelt there.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
This is the same ground the family had already covered. Generations earlier “Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son’s son, and Sarai his daughter in law, his son Abram’s wife; and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan; and they came unto Haran, and dwelt there.”

Terah brought Abram up from Ur along the Euphrates and stopped at Haran. Now Jacob, coming out of Canaan, goes north and east and finds shepherds who say, “Of Haran are we.” Jacob’s road runs back to the family’s old dwelling.

precepts.text: Terah begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran; Laban is of Nahor's line, so Jacob has come to his own people.
precepts.point: This ties the family line together: Abraham first journeyed from Ur of the Chaldees northwest to Haran, and now Jacob comes up from Canaan northeast to Haran. Because of the way Jacob traveled, he went back home and is dwelling amongst family.

note.label: Genesis 29: Bone and Flesh in Haran

precepts.why:
“Know ye Laban the son of Nahor?” And the men of Haran know him. “Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran.” Laban is of Nahor’s line, and he dwells in that area because the family remained there when Terah stopped at Haran.

It ties the family line together. Abraham first journeyed from Ur of the Chaldees northwest to Haran, and now Jacob comes up from Canaan northeast to Haran. Because of the way Jacob traveled, he went back home and is dwelling amongst family, the house of Nahor.

precepts.text: The whole earth was of one language and one speech, showing a tongue is a language and a dialect.
precepts.point: Because Israel was scattered among nations whose tongue they did not understand, the Most High spoke to his people with stammering lips and another tongue. The cloven tongues were the many languages of the lands where Israel was dispersed, and they spoke the word of the Most High in them like fire.

note.label: Acts 2: Pentecost and the Scattered House of Israel

precepts.why:
Cloven means split or divided, and tongues means dialects, languages and speech. Go back to Babel and the word defines itself: “And the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech.” A tongue is a language. It is not the unknown babble the Pentecostal and Baptist churches practice.

The front of the King James Bible itself says it was translated out of the original tongues, meaning Hebrew and Greek, different languages. That is what a tongue is in the scriptures.

The glossolalia established in the churches in the late 1800s and 1900s is a pagan spirit giving utterance, the spirit of Satan, not the Holy Ghost. You cannot learn or teach the knowledge of the Most High through babble that no one can interpret. What sat on the apostles was divided languages, real speech, so the word could be taught.
